content.text: Book reference: Chapter 7, pages 205–238. Guided Exercises: Managing File System Permissions from the Command Line, Managing Default Permissions and File Access. Lab: Controlling Access to Files.
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — This whole chapter

Reading, setting, and reasoning about permissions — including special permissions and umask — is core RHCSA material tested directly and constantly relied on in every later chapter (services, networking, storage all lean on correct permissions).

Every file has exactly one owning user and one owning group. Permissions are set separately for three categories — owning user, owning group, and everyone else ("other") — and the most specific category that applies to you wins: your user permissions override your group permissions, which override other.
Directory's file names can be listed
Files inside can be created or deleted
Can be run as a command
Directory can be entered (cd) and its files accessed, if their own permissions allow it
💡 Why this matters — Why directories need both r and x to be useful

r alone on a directory lets you list file names but nothing else about them (no sizes, dates, or permissions, and you can't open them even if you already know a name). x alone lets you access a file inside if you already know its exact name, but you can't list what's there at all. Normal usable directory access needs both together — r+x is the practical minimum for "browse this directory."
⚠ WARNING — Deleting a file is a directory permission, not a file permission

Anyone with write permission on the directory containing a file can delete that file — regardless of the file's own permissions or who owns it. This surprises people coming from Windows. (The sticky bit, covered below, is the one exception.)

Linux permissions on a directory are NOT inherited by new subdirectories or files automatically — they only affect access to that one directory itself, though restrictive permissions higher up the tree can still block reaching what's below.
File type: - regular file, d directory, l soft link (b/c/p/s = device or special files)

rfile1 is owned by user database1, group consultant1, permissions -rw-rw-r--. User operator1 (who is a member of consultant1 but not the owner) can therefore read AND write it — group permissions apply since he's not the owning user. User database2 (in neither the owning user nor the owning group) only gets the other row — read only.
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — The trap: group permission can be MORE restrictive than other

If a file is -rw-r--rw- (group has only read, other has read+write), a member of the owning group is still capped at read — even though a random unrelated user would have write. Most-specific-applies means YOUR most specific category applies, whether it happens to be more generous or more restrictive than a broader one. Don't assume group access is always ≥ other access.
chmod WhoWhatWhich file — Who = u/g/o/a (user/group/other/all), What = +/-/= (add/remove/set exactly), Which = r/w/x.
chmod go-rw file1 # remove read+write from group and other
chmod a+x file2 # add execute for everyone
chmod -R g+rwX demodir # recursive; capital X only adds execute to directories, or to files that already have execute somewhere
⚠ WARNING — Capital X vs lowercase x in recursive chmod

Lowercase x would blindly make every plain data file executable too. Capital X is the safe recursive choice: it sets execute on directories (so they stay navigable) and on files that already have execute for someone, but leaves ordinary non-executable files alone.
Each of the three digits (user, group, other) is a sum: read=4, write=2, execute=1.
chmod 644 samplefile # rw-r--r-- (owner read/write, everyone else read-only)
chmod 750 sampledir # rwxr-x--- (owner full, group read+enter, other nothing)
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Numeric is what experienced admins actually type

Faster to type and say aloud than the symbolic form, and it sets the complete permission set in one shot — worth being fully fluent translating in both directions (750 → rwxr-x--- and back) without a calculator.
Change owning group (root, or the file's own owner if they belong to that group)
Recursively, through a whole directory tree
Change owning group only — same effect as chown :group
⚠ WARNING — Always use a colon, never a period, in owner:group

chown owner.group file is a legacy syntax that still works but is genuinely ambiguous: a period is a VALID character inside a username. If a user literally named enoch.root exists, chown enoch.root file could be interpreted as that single username rather than user enoch, group root — with no error, just the wrong result. The colon form is unambiguous because a colon can never appear in a username. Always use the colon.

sections.title: 7.3 Special permissions — setuid, setgid, sticky bit

content.text: Recognizing these in an ls -l listing, and setting/removing them yourself, is directly tested — this is not optional background material.
Runs as the file's owning user, not whoever ran it
Runs as the file's owning group
New files inside inherit the DIRECTORY's group, not the creating user's primary group
Users can only delete their OWN files here, even with directory write access

Classic real examples: /usr/bin/passwd is setuid root (so any user can update their own encrypted entry in the root-owned /etc/shadow); /usr/bin/locate is setgid slocate; /tmp has the sticky bit so any user can create files there but nobody can delete someone else's.
s where owner's x would be (e.g. rws)
setuid set — lowercase s means execute was also set, uppercase S means execute was NOT set for owner
s where group's x would be
setgid set — same uppercase/lowercase execute-present rule
t where other's x would be
sticky bit set — lowercase t = execute present for other, uppercase T = not present
chmod g+s directory # symbolic: add setgid
chmod 2770 directory # numeric: leading 2 = setgid, then rwxrwx---
💡 Why this matters — Why setgid on a shared directory is the standard collaboration trick

New files normally inherit the CREATING USER's primary group — usually their own private group, which nobody else can access. Setgid on the shared directory overrides that: every new file automatically belongs to the directory's group instead, so a whole team keeps working on shared files without anyone needing to remember to chgrp manually after every single file they create.
New files and directories don't start from nothing — they start from a fixed baseline, then get restricted by your shell's umask:
0666 (rw-rw-rw-) — execute is never included by default, even after umask, specifically so a compromised service can't accidentally create and immediately run a malicious file
umask is a bitmask of permissions to REMOVE from that starting point — the opposite sense from chmod. A umask digit works the same 4/2/1 arithmetic as chmod, but subtracts rather than adds.

umask alone (no argument) shows the current shell's value; umask 027 sets it for that shell session only. The default is normally 002 when a regular user's UID is ≥200 and their username matches their primary group name (the standard user-private-group setup), or 022 otherwise.
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Making a umask change permanent

A bare umask 027 typed at the prompt only lasts for that one shell. To persist it for one user, add the line to their ~/.bashrc. To change it system-wide, create a new file under /etc/profile.d/ (e.g. /etc/profile.d/local-umask.sh) containing the umask command — and remember the user must log out and back in for it to take effect; it does not apply retroactively to already-open shells.

sections.title: Hands-on: practice these on your own lab

content.text: 1. ssh student@servera, mkdir permtest, touch permtest/file1 — check its default permissions with ls -l.
2. chmod 640 permtest/file1; chmod u+x permtest/file1; ls -l to watch the mode change both ways.
3. sudo groupadd -g 30500 sharedteam; sudo chown :sharedteam permtest; sudo chmod g+s permtest — confirm the setgid s shows in ls -ld permtest.
4. As a different member of sharedteam, create a file inside permtest and confirm it inherits the sharedteam group automatically, without anyone running chgrp.
5. umask 027; touch permtest/tightfile; ls -l to see the tighter default; then umask 002 to restore the normal default for the rest of your session.
6. ls -ld /tmp — find the sticky bit t and connect it back to why two different users can both create files there but never delete each other's.
1. Q1 — A file is -rw-r--rw-, owned by alice:staff. Bob is in the staff group but isn't alice. Can bob write to this file? Why or why not?

2. Q2 — You want everyone on a shared team to automatically get group-write on new files created in one specific directory, without each person remembering to chmod every time. What single permission solves this, and where do you set it?
3. Q3 — Convert the permission string rwxr-xr-- to its three-digit octal form.

Q1 — No. Bob matches the GROUP category (staff), which here is r-- (read only) — more restrictive than other's rw- in this example. Most-specific-applies means bob is capped at group permissions even though a random unrelated user would actually have write access here.

Q2 — setgid (g+s / numeric leading 2) on the shared directory. New files then inherit the directory's group automatically instead of the creating user's own primary group, so the whole team keeps write access without manual chgrp after every file.
Every file has one owning user and one owning group; the most specific matching category (user > group > other) is the one that applies to you.

chmod changes permissions symbolically (u/g/o/a, +/-/=, r/w/x) or numerically (4/2/1 per digit); chown/chgrp change ownership — always with a colon, never a period, when setting user and group together.

setuid/setgid/sticky (numeric 4/2/1 as a leading fourth digit) are special permissions: setuid/setgid change what identity a program runs as (or what group new files in a directory inherit); sticky restricts deletion in a shared directory to each file's own owner.
New files start at 0666, new directories at 0777, before umask subtracts permissions from that baseline; ~/.bashrc persists a umask per user, /etc/profile.d/ persists it system-wide.
